question: A neonate is born at 38 weeks gestation age via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 40-year-old woman. The mother was working in South America when she discovered that she was pregnant. She had 2 days of fever associated with cough and swollen cervical glands, which resolved spontaneously at 12 weeks gestation prior to returning to the United States. The mother has no current symptoms. Neonatal examination shows weight and length at the 8th percentile, and head circumference below the 3rd percentile for age. Heart and lung sounds are normal. There is moderate hepatosplenomegaly. Skin examination shows diffuse, dark-blue papules and nodules. Serology from the mother and infant are attained. Which of the following serology patterns is most consistent with a suspected congenital infection? lgM levels lgG levels lgM levels lgG levels in the in the in the in the mother mother newborn newborn

options.text: gM levels lgG levels lgM levels lgG levels in the in the in the in the mother mother newborn newborn x @ A

explanation.text: Growth restriction, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, and a diffuse dark-blue rash (ie, blueberry muffin rash) are nonspecific features shared by multiple congenital (TORCH) infections (eg, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella). These infections are transmitted transplacentally to the fetus from a mother infected during pregnancy. Although maternal symptoms may be mild (eg, fever, lymphadenopathy), the developing fetus can have significant morbidity, particularly with a first trimester infection. Serology and polymerase chain reaction testing can help to determine the diagnosis in a neonate with suspected intrauterine infection. Neonatal antibody titers can be difficult to interpret, particularly due to maternal transfer of some antibodies and not others: • Maternal lgM does not cross the placenta, so detection of organism-speafic lgM in a symptomatic neonate is diagnostic. • At birth, virtually all infant lgG is maternally derived lgG that crossed the placenta, and elevated maternal lgG would be expected in this mother with infectious symptoms 6-7 months prior to delivery (Choices A and D). Therefore, organism-specific newborn lgG (eg, Toxoplasma lgG) will also be elevated in the setting of a past maternal infection.

(Choice C) Maternal lgM may be negative with a remote infection (as with this mother) or positive if recently infected. False negative lgM titers can also occur in neonates with congenital infection whose lgM waned before birth or in those who have yet to form a robust immune response. However, a positive newborn lgG would be expected due to transplacental transfer of maternal lgG.

educational_objective: Organism-specific lgM is diagnostic of congenital infection in a symptomatic neonate (eg, growth restriction, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, blueberry muffin rash). Because maternal lgG titers are expected with a past infection and neonatal lgG at birth is maternally derived, elevated newborn lgG is also expected.
